This game is the ultimate Batman (super hero genre) experience for me. Ever since the mediocre Gotham Knights and the disastrous SS:KTJL, I'm in love with this trilogy even more than before. Many people don't care about super hero genre and also don't like it. I was one of those people once. I didn't care about Batman at all. I always thought he was just a boring grumpy guy dressed as a bat. Until in 2009 Rocksteady started this franchise and I fell in love with the world they created. You can't find any batman's story in other medias like this one. It's dark and gritty. It has great heroes, villains, anti-heroes and most important of all great character development for each of them. And don't let me tell you about the masterfully crafted freeflow combat alongside the amazing stealth and puzzle/detective gameplay of this masterpiece. Arkham Knight is the latest installment in the series (we don't count that live service crap) and even after 9 years this game still looks breathtaking and better than a lot of AAA 9th gen games. Some people criticize the addition of Batmobile to the series and think it's overused but I personally always love to EVEN THE ODDS if you know what I mean (Wink Wink).
I give this masterpiece a 9/10 and the only reason this isn't a 10/10 for me is that the boosfights were a little bit underwhelming and had a lot more potential. :)

PS: RIP Kevin Conroy. You will always be Batman in my heart <3

Played it for around an hour so far.

The combat is fun and responsive, the gliding is great and the game looks okay (AF is set to 4 by default which makes some textures look awful).  That's the good parts.

The bad parts are the framerate issues which are all over the place and the batmobile.  The game will frequently pause or dip to sub 10 fps on a gtx 970 when entering or approaching new areas.  Cutscenes have similar issues to witcher 3 in that while in engine they run at even less fps (by default the game itself is locked to 30, tweakable in the ini files) than the normal game making them stutter or appear stilted.

Summoning the batmobile causes major frame rate drops.  At one point I summoned the car to try the batmobile takedown move.  By the time the frame rate recovered the batmobile had crushed the pack of guys I was fighting including the Riddler henchman I wanted to interrogate.

The batmobile itself handles awfully.  There are forced batmobile sections which involve chasing targets such as tanks or vehicles.  The handling makes some turns difficult to pull off and the vehicle feels clunky.  Some have recommended turning into a tank for a small amount of time for more precise control but this kills all momentum.  Tank mode is really boring but necessary to take out armored vehicles.  If you eject while under attack from armored vehicles batman will get upset someone is wrecking his car.  There doesn't appear to be a way (yet) to deal with vehicles without the batmobile which ruins the feel of the prior batman games.  Hopefully the need for the batmobile is limited later in the game.

Unless this is patched soon it's definitely a refund.  I bought the game based on the prior Rocksteady Batman titles which played well on launch but this is a terrible PC port.  Never really expected the game to turn out this way but I guess alarm bells should have triggered when there was no PC review prior to launch.

The story continues from the last game in the chronology. Hands down it has the best hand to hand combat in any batman. Environmental takedowns too. The old WB never disappointed me, I love their Middle Earth games so much. Great DLCs too.

Other than the photorealistic next gen graphics that even current modern AAA games fail to deliver, the whole open world game is full of great contents. You love Warthog & Scorpion of Master Chief? Wait till you try the Batmobile! :o

But there were some minor yet bothering issues I just couldn't ignore. First, the Anti-aliasing in this game is nuts. I recommend the use of frame gen and LS1 sharpening via LSFG program. Disable mouse smoothing too. But the worst part is, the game wants you to grind every piece of 200+ puzzles scattered around the city to even watch the ending :(

Only 8.5% players did that grind. Others simply watched the ending in YouTube! If you love grinding puzzles around then you are in luck.

[b]Although I'm losing my interest in fancy cinematic heroes as an Adult, I think this title truly deserves everyone's attention. Its too good.[/b]

Says I have over 1300 hours in this game, lol, so that gives me some experience with it, right?  Isn't it great how people post reviews with an hour or less on a game?  Ridiculous.

Anyway, since this came out in 2015, and I am writing a review in 2022, I am a bit behind the times.  But I had a lot of free times these past few years due to an injury, and I been playing a lot of games.  Almost every game, TBH.   Batman Arkham Knight is incredible, even 7 years later after its release.  I have a high end PC, so I have all the graphic options maxed, but this game still looks amazing after 7 years.  Anyone that is a fan of Batman, and does not have this game, you need to get it.  Story is really good, voice acting is near best of any game out there, which makes the story even better.  And its just plain fun  being Batman.  Once you start leveling up and getting most of the skills unlocked, you can really feel the power of this character.

Easily by far the best Batman game out there.  And it pains me that there won't be a sequel.  To me, it's like all the previous Batman games were practice for the developers to get this perfect gem of a game made.  

One thing I did find comical, is this game takes place during a single terrible night in Gotham.  Ummmm....I may not be the worlds greatest detective, but I just can't seem to figure out how 1300 hours fits into a 12 hour night.

1300 hours....and I still play it.

Get it.

Batman: Arkham Knight (AK) is the final installment in the popular Arkham franchise. Putting the player in the shoes of the Caped Crusader, Batman will be facing his greatest challenge yet that could change Gotham City and himself forever. Does this grand conclusion live up to the hype? Let’s dive in.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
- Addicting and satisfying combat system
- Brilliantly designed stealth sections 
- Large open world with gorgeous environments
- Tons of sidequests and puzzles to tackle
- The introduction of the Batmobile completely redefines the game
- A faithful adaptation that respects Batman’s mythology

[h2]Cons[/h2]
- The lack of/terrible boss battles

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Generally, you will be doing one of this three stuff in AK: beating up thugs using the FreeFlow Combat system, silently picking enemies off one by one in Predator sections or cruising around the decrepit city of Gotham. Each of them also receives substantial new additions (which will be covered in a separate section), giving more flexibility to the players on how to approach the situation.

Firstly, let’s begin with the combat. A staple of the franchise, it is more rhythm-based and emphasizes strategic offense compared to other action titles. After hitting an enemy three times, Batman will enter into a FreeFlow state where every hit will instantly knock them to the ground. As most of the fights have you engaging with more than a dozen enemies at the same time, the combat system allows Batman to gracefully moves across the battlefield at lightning speed. 

To counter this, the goons will come equipped with a wide variety of equipment to hinder your assault. For example, enemies armed with knives must be dodged multiple times while the ones with stun batons can only be attacked from behind. There are also special enemy types such as the brutes that can tank a lot of hits and the medic that can revive downed enemies. 

Moving on, we have Predator AKA the stealth levels. During these sections, the mooks are all armed with guns; therefore, instead of engaging them head-on, Batman will instead take all of them out silently. Creativity is encouraged here as there are numerous ways to take down an enemy. Sure, you could just choke them from behind, but it would be much more fun to smash them through a window, grab them while hanging from a ledge or even surprise them from a vent. While playing FreeFlow makes you feel like an unstoppable beast, Predator on the other hand reminds you exactly why Batman is feared by the superstitious and cowardly lot. 

Just like normal combat, AK will challenge your sneaking skills by having the enemies adapt to your tactics. Take out too many lone gunmen? They will hunt you down in pairs. Attacking from above? They will place mines on possible vantage points. Certain enemies also have unique gadgets including wearing camouflage suits that make spotting them harder or operating a drone with a large cone of vision.

As the legendary Batman, you will have an assortment of gadgets available at any time. From jamming guns using the disruptor to mimicking audio with the voice synthesizer, these devices will greatly assist you as most of them can be used in either FreeFlow or Predator sections. All of these features are seamlessly integrated into gameplay to provide an exhilarating experience and prevent the game from being repetitive.

Last, but certainly not least, is exploration. Gotham City is a huge concrete jungle surrounded by three islands. Thus, the game is richly-filled with tons of optional content to tackle, ranging from solving intricate riddles to dismantling a supervillain’s career with the Most Wanted side missions. 

And while we are on the topic of the playground that is Gotham, the graphics in AK are incredibly appealing to look at. Neon signs can be spotted from a mile away, skyscrapers being bombarded with billboards, and transit rail weaves around buildings; the city has never felt more alive. Moreover, the facial animations look stunning for a game released in 2015 and the attention to detail towards the environments (especially Batman’s suits) is staggering.

[h1]New Features[/h1]
AK introduced a great deal of new stuff that warranted its own section. To kick things off, let’s cover the biggest addition: the almighty Batmobile. With two different modes, this monster of a tank completely transformed every aspect of the game; pursuit mode is designed for high-speed chases while battle mode is for fighting armored vehicles. Apart from that, it can also be utilized for solving puzzles and analyzing forensics.

FreeFlow and Predator also receive significant upgrades to spice things up. For the former, the DualPlay mechanic allows you to switch instantly to another character (Robin, Nightwing and Catwoman) in the heat of combat without any interruption. The latter introduced the Fear Takedowns, a powerful move that allows Batman to incapacitate up to five goons in seconds. In addition, both modes also incorporated environmental takedowns that are one-hit-knockouts towards any enemy.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Set a year after Arkham City, Batman, while still heroic, is not as calm as he used to be after the events of the last game. To make matters worse, it is Halloween night and a familiar face resurfaces: Jonathan Crane AKA Scarecrow. Along with the support of every supervillain in town, he is also backed by the Arkham Knight, a mysterious figure who has an endless supply of militia men behind him and knows every secret about the Dark Knight. 

The overall execution of the plot is enjoyable. While certain plot twists are quite predictable and there are certain moments where the game forced you to violate your common sense, the characterization of the characters is done respectfully to the source material. For instance, Batman is accurately portrayed as the nigh-unstoppable badass that he is, but AK also deconstructed and discussed issues regarding his character such as his unwillingness to kill and trust issues with his allies.

Despite saying that, the Most Wanted side missions focusing on each villain personally is a massive letdown. What I am expecting is a penultimate showdown where Batman dukes it out with his supervillain in a one-on-one battle. Instead, most of them are taken down instantly without any resistance, either by a QTE or during a cutscene. 

[b]The Rest[/b]
[list]
[*] Completing missions give you XP for leveling up. Gaining one level rewards you with one upgrade point that can be used to unlock new abilities or boost preexisting ones.
[*] AR challenges are a series of trials to hone your skills in the game. Be warned as they are difficult and designed for experienced players.
[*] Environmental destruction is implemented for the first time here. Run over gates, concrete beams and freaking trees for mayhem.
[*] Enemy chatter. The Arkham series is probably the only franchise where I actively listen to the thugs’ dialogue because of how hilarious they are.
[/list]

[h1]Playtime, Replayability and Achievements[/h1]
[b]Playtime:[/b] It took me around 90 hours to 100% the game on Normal difficulty. A sizeable chunk is also spent getting high scores on AR challenges.

[b]Replayability:[/b] Immensely. As mentioned above, the AR challenges alone are enough to keep you occupied for a dozen hours.

[b]Achievements:[/b] A grand total of 113. Most are obtained simply by completing quests. Others required a lot more effort and luck like completing a specific level without taking any damage.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
No matter if you are a fan of the comics, the animated series or the movies, Arkham Knight is perfect for you. With excellent gameplay and gorgeous graphics, Rocksteady capped off the epic finale of the franchise with a bang. Become vengeance. Become the night. Become The Batman.

 Boss Battles: The epic and creative boss battles of previous games in the series (e.g., Mr. Freeze) have been replaced in this game by more Batmobile/Tank battles.

Despite its flaws, Batman: Arkham Knight is one of the best superhero games ever made, perhaps even the best. If you set aside the Batmobile and tanking, its storytelling and character development make it a masterpiece.

[b]Arkham Knight[/b] is the final game in the main [b]Arkham[/b] series and the only one to be released on the eighth generation of video game consoles. Naturally, everybody waited for it back in the days, but... let's just say that this one debuted with a major scandal. On start, the game was so bugged and terribly optimized (as long as we're talking about personal computers, of course, since console releases weren't nearly as bad) that... it was actually pulled from [b]Steam[/b], following thousands of negative reviews. Imagine [b]PlayStation 4[/b] version of [b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b] and you'll get the idea 'bout how it was with this game on start. Thankfully, unlike [b]CD Projekt RED[/b] who, at the moment I write this review, still fail to get their sh*t together and fix their product, [b]Rocksteady[/b] soon brought the game back and, I must say, it's my most favorite game in the series now. Simple like that. Even though I'm far from being a big fan of [b]Arkham[/b] games, this one? It's my favorite one.

Why? Well, first of all, presentation this time is absolutely fantastic. It always was like that in the [b]Arkham[/b] series, but honestly, the next-gen presentation is... you know... [i]next-gen[/i]. And on personal computers? Boy, oh, boy, this game can easily blow your mind. Seeing the [b]Arkham Knight[/b] in [b]4K[/b] with some extra features from [b]NVIDIA[/b] (like ray tracing and the enhanced rain)? Years later, it still feels absolutely breathtaking. Add godlike design, the fact that [b]Mark Hamill[/b] has finally returned to play [b]Joker[/b] (in case you forgot, he was replaced with [b]Troy Baker[/b] in spin-offs) and the best story in the series, and you'll see why it's really, [i]really[/i] hard for me not to like this game. But naturally, the great presentation is not why I consider this game to be the best.

You see, [b]Arkham Knight[/b] is pretty much what [b]Arkham City[/b] was supposed to be back in the days. Sure, a lot of people enjoyed [b]Arkham City[/b]. Like... [i]a lot[/i]. But it was also hard to argue with the fact that it was ultimately empty, traveling the world used to quickly get boring, optional goals were extremely confusing without any reason and so on. [b]Arkham Knight[/b]? It fixes most of those problems. For example, the world in [b]Arkham Knight[/b] (like in [b]Arkham Origins[/b], we're dealing with [b]Gotham[/b] here) is filled with a fair share of open world activities. Sure, most of those are extremely generic (save the hostages, disarm the bombs, deactivate the towers, capture the outposts / checkpoints and so on), but still, we finally got [b]Arkham[/b] game with a proper open world environment. The one that is not just a gimmick, The missions became less frustrating too, we've got proper markers on map but, most importantly, we've got [b]Batmobile[/b].

I mean, we already had it in previous games, but this time it'll be a real deal. Which means that we'll be free to summon and control it at pretty much every moment with some obvious exceptions. And that's where the real fun begins. Sure, not everybody loved [b]Batmobile[/b], but it sure added heck of a lot of stuff. From races and tactical battles on streets of [b]Gotham[/b] (which eliminates the problem with boring travels almost completely) to the new tools and puzzles. Talking about puzzles, by the way. Even though I do consider [b]Arkham Knight[/b] to be the best game in the series, it's also kind of amazing just how stupid [b]Rocksteady[/b] can be.

Let's forget about [b]Arkham Knight[/b] for a moment and look back. What everybody (even the die-hard fans of the series) hated about [b]Arkham[/b] series the most? It's [b]Batman[/b], right? [i]Right?[/i] OK, OK, it was [b]Riddler[/b]. As long as we're not talking about the mobile spin-offs, every bloody game used to include hundreds of [i]extremely[/i] annoying collectibles. I mean, having such the annoying collectibles alone is a [i]huge[/i] problem (seriously, [b]Nigma[/b]'s stuff is the most annoying collectibles I've ever seen in my entire life), but having [i]hundreds[/i] of them? In every... bloody... game? It was a joke. When [b]Arkham City[/b] added even more of those and made them even more annoying? It was like [i]FFFUUUUUUUUUU.......[/i] Now, what did [b]Rocksteady[/b] do in this game? Well, they've reduced the amount of collectibles from [b]440[/b] to [b]243[/b] (about the same amount with [b]Arkham Asylum[/b], which had [b]240[/b]), sure, but... they've actually made those collectibles [i]even more[/i] annoying by... involving the [b]Batmobile[/b].

I mean, come on, guys! Wasting a lot of time on a single “puzzle” that didn't even felt satisfying in any way, felt awful, but wasting even more because now we're supposed to deal with the car? That, I must add, comes with some weird [b]HALO[/b]-like controls? Screw that. Naturally, after so many games and so many [b]Riddler[/b]'s crap, you'll want to just ignore it, but guess what? [i]Surpri-i-i-i-ise![/i] You can't. Well, as long as you want the real ending that is. That's right. The only way to actually get the real ending in this game... is to collect / solve... all [b]243[/b]... [b]Riddler[/b]'s... nonsense... And then do some crappy challenges. Because reasons. [i]WHAT WERE THEY THINKING?!![/i] It's not even like [b]Rocksteady[/b] refused to listen to the feedback. It's like they did listen and, instead of improving, decided to make everybody suffer. [i]On purpose[/i]. [i]WHAT... WERE... THEY... THINKING?!![/i] Were they actually taken hostages by [b]Nigma[/b]? I literally can't find any other explanation for such crappy decision.

Aside from that, though, [b]Arkham Knight[/b] is an open world [b]Batman[/b] game we all deserved back in [b]2011[/b]. It still isn't perfect, of course. Far from it. Especially thanks to some clunky [b]Batmobile[/b] controls (I actually have a friend who disliked the entire game just because of that), way too generic activities and the fact that pretty much all optional missions (even those that you're supposed to buy separately) feel like more of exactly the same stuff we've already seen in previous games, [i]but[/i] at the same exact time the road action, proper open world environment and stunning next-gen visuals, together with the story that will please both the [b]Arkham[/b] fans and dedicated comic book readers (you'll actually need to do some research to fully understand the true ending here, so, hope you're familiar with at least the most famous [b]Batman[/b] comics) sure makes [b]Arkham Knight[/b] the very best thing from [b]Rocksteady[/b]. At least, in my eyes.

Even the most of the technical issues were fixed at the moment I write this. Well, not all of them, of course (the game still hates wireless gamepads, while the interactive fog/smoke feature from [b]NVIDIA[/b] is completely broken up to this day and will make the game crash to desktop during the certain parts), but still, we can all just forget about failed initial release and enjoy the game in its ultimate form. And naturally, there's a lot to enjoy here. Like [b]Arkham Asylum[/b], [b]Arkham Knight[/b] is one of those games that totally worth your time just because of the presentation, but this time there's actually quite a lot of optional fun to have here. And even though not all of it feels good enough, well... you've got the idea. The game also comes with some surprisingly nice story [b]DLC[/b] (some of which will even let you play characters like [b]Batgirl[/b] and [b]Harley Quinn[/b]) and even the skins this time are surprisingly exciting. You want the suit and [b]Batmobile[/b] from [b]Tim Burton[/b]'s movies? Or maybe even [b]Batmobile[/b] from [b]1966[/b] series? [b]Arkham Knight[/b] is here to deliver. Like I said, even though this game is not perfect, there's [i]a lot[/i] of good here. Dixi.

When I played Arkham Origins, I thought it was a fine game with some notable flaws that made it inferior to Arkham City, but all would be made right with the release of Arkham Knight. But that's not exactly what happened -- instead, I think Arkham Knight is a fine game with some notable flaws that make it inferior to Arkham City.

Let's tackle the first elephant in the room: the botched port and initial release. It stank up Steam so bad that it single-handedly [strike]kickstarted[/strike] popularized the refund policy ([i]thanks to Link XL1 for pointing out refunds actually started a bit earlier than AK[/i]), and it was the reason I held off on actually buying it until a good long while had passed, despite being a massive fan of the series. I can be brief about this: my brand new rig has 16 GB of memory and a GTX 1070, and the game runs at a near-constant 70 FPS at 1440p maxed settings while looking absolutely gorgeous. Now, I get that not everyone has had that experience, or will have that experience, but I can only judge the game on how it plays for me at this point in time, and I have no reason to complain. That's not to say I tihnk that putting out a release as broken as this one is in any way acceptable or excusable -- it's not -- but I'm not going to count it against the game in its current state.

The same can't be said for elephant number two, which is the Batmobile. The Dynamic Duo in this game isn't Batman and Robin, but Batman and his amazing rooftop-hopping car. It quickly veers from cool into silly and contrived, and about the only thing missing is the Batmobile doing inverted takedowns (it [i]does[/i] hang upside down a few times, so that's not as implausible as it sounds...). They made sure you can't miss out on the experience by putting in vehicular combat and puzzles that require the Batmobile, but I found myself more frustrated than entertained by these sections. Despite what the game designers thought, it would have been completely fine if the Batmobile had just been there as a cooler way of getting you from A to B. Throw in the optional racetracks for the people who like that sort of thing, I'm fine with that. Have maybe [i]one[/i] sequence where the Batmobile gets to slug it out with a tank or helicopter, sure. But repeated vehicular combat sequences and painfully forced puzzle sequences just detract from the experience. While you can avoid almost all racing and puzzles if you just don't go after the Riddler (as if!) the tank battles are there to stay. It's as if someone baked you a delicious, velvety smooth chocolate cake, except that they mixed in crunchy peanuts to chip your teeth on, because they read somewhere that chocolate and peanuts go well together.

There are a lot of things Arkham Knight gets right, too. The meat and potatoes of the game, combat and predator encounters, work as smooth as ever, and there are the requisite tweaks and new moves to keep things interesting without completely unbalancing things like the shock gloves in Origins did. There's a smorgasbord of villains on the loose in Gotham waiting for you to arrest them, and they all involve different gameplay, so you can easily mix things up without getting bored. The voice acting is top notch, both from the regulars and the guest villains (special tip of the hat to Dwight Schultz, who plays a terrifying Professor Pyg -- I was surprised to find out it was him when I looked it up). The story is engaging, and I'm happy to say that's still the case even if you had the identity of the Arkham Knight spoiled before you picked up the game, like I did. I especially like the way the writers justified the issue of Batman suddenly deciding to stick massive guns on his Batmobile (even if they do conveniently fire "non-lethal rounds" when targeting humans). If this sounds a bit out of character for Batman, it's because it is... and you'll find out why as you play the game. Having said that, I'm definitely not a fan of the ending (the true ending you get with 100% completion), which is deliberately ambiguous on the ultimate fate of Batman and Gotham. It's not terrible, I can live with it, but it still feels like a cop-out and something the writers could absolutely have avoided in favor of a stronger statement. As a cap to the whole series, it's a bit underwhelming.

Arkham Knight gets an easy "recommended" from me, but it's not as great as the final installment could have been.

[b]Batman: Arkham Knight isn’t just a game, it’s an experience. [h1]The Story – Fear, Madness, and Closure[/h1]
[b]Set nine months after Arkham City, Gotham is once again in chaos, this time thanks to Scarecrow, who’s planning to blanket the city with his fear toxin on Halloween night. But the twist? There’s a new masked menace in town, the Arkham Knight, a militarized, vengeful version of Batman himself who seems to know every one of Bruce’s secrets. The mystery around his identity builds beautifully until that moment of revelation hits (and for comic fans, it’s a rewarding one).[/b]

[b]And then there’s The Joker. Yes, he’s dead, but he’s also more alive than ever inside Batman’s mind. The hallucinations and constant taunts from him add a psychological layer to the story that makes it both heartbreaking and fascinating. You’re not just fighting Gotham’s villains, you’re fighting Batman’s sanity. That inner struggle between fear, guilt, and control gives the narrative its true soul.
By the end, with the Knightfall Protocol and its haunting finale, you’re left with the perfect mix of closure and curiosity. Did Bruce really die? Or did he finally become the legend Gotham needed? It’s the kind of ending that lingers with you long after the credits roll.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay and the Batmobile – A Love-Hate Relationship[/h1]
[b]The addition of the Batmobile was one of the biggest highlights of Arkham Knight. For the first time, you can drive the Batmobile through Gotham, and wow, it feels incredible… until it starts to feel like a tank simulator. The two modes, Pursuit and Battle, make it versatile, speeding through neon-lit streets feels exhilarating, while engaging in tank battles with drone armies can be fun… but also a little repetitive.
Still, there’s something special about hearing that engine roar, activating afterburners, and charging through the city in the rain. It’s the Batmobile we always dreamed of, even if it occasionally overstays its welcome.[/b]

[h1]Visuals and Performance – Beauty and the Bug[/h1]
[b]On a technical level, this game was way ahead of its time. The level of detail in Gotham, the lighting, the rain effects on Batman’s armor, it’s breathtaking. Fun fact: a single character model in Arkham Knight had more polygons than the entire Arkham Asylum environment! That’s insane dedication to realism.
But then there’s the elephant in the Batcave, the PC port. The launch was rough, to put it mildly. Frame drops, crashes, texture bugs, you name it. It was so bad that Warner Bros. actually pulled it from Steam for a while. Thankfully, it’s much better now, but at launch, it was Gotham’s biggest crime.[/b]

[h1]Voice Acting and Atmosphere – Legends Return[/h1]
[b]Having Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill return as Batman and Joker was like the emotional backbone of the entire game. Their performances elevate every scene, from Bruce’s weary voice of resolve to Joker’s chaotic banter that dances between funny and disturbing. These two are Batman and Joker. No question.
Gotham City itself feels alive, even in its evacuation. The rain, the reflections, the distant thunder, it’s the perfect gothic stage for Batman’s last act.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Epic conclusion to one of gaming’s best trilogies
[*]Deep, emotional story with strong psychological themes
[*]Beautiful visuals and atmospheric world design
[*]Outstanding voice performances by Conroy and Hamill
[*]The Batmobile is awesome when used in moderation
[*]A truly satisfying (and haunting) ending
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The PC port had serious technical issues at launch
[*]Overuse of the Batmobile in certain missions
[*]Some repetitive combat and tank battles
[/list]
[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
[b]Batman: Arkham Knight isn’t perfect, but it doesn’t need to be. It’s ambitious, bold, and emotionally charged, the kind of finale that leaves a mark. It’s a story about fear, identity, and legacy told through some of the best writing, acting, and gameplay the genre has ever seen.
For me, this game wasn’t just another title to complete, it was a journey. One that made me admire Batman even more and reminded me why the Arkham series will forever be legendary.
10/10 – A masterpiece of storytelling and atmosphere. The Dark Knight couldn’t have asked for a better send-off.[/b]

The Arkham series will always hold a special place in my heart, Asylum was a genre defining game with a superb beat em up style that marks the beginning of a great franchise, City improves upon the first game in every way imaginable and has a kicker of a story to boot, Origins offers a strong cast of villains and highly memorable boss battles. With the release of Arkham Knight, fans of the franchise are expecting a proper sendoff to the Arkham franchise, did it deliver?

For the most part it did, the game looks absolutely stunning and plays incredibly smooth without any problems whatsoever, granted I played this game over a year after its horrendous launch plagued by a myriad of bugs and crashes, among other issues. But after the updates, the game has little to no bugs whatsoever. You can tell that Rocksteady put all their hearts into the creation of this game, every bit of Gotham is brimming with detail and feels colorful despite the dark and gritty undertone of the game itself. Character models are beautifully designed and the voice acting from each character are superb. Despite all its positives, most people found the game to not be a proper sendoff to the Arkham series as it did not meet their expectations. Why?

For starters, my main gripe about this game is the heavy emphasis on the bat mobile, sure it’s fun to drive every once in a while, but the game shoves it at your face every 15 minutes and create stupidly complex scenarios that requires you to use the bat mobile. For example, [spoiler]why would the Riddler create racetracks for Batman to race on? Why would Deathstroke use a tank to fight Batman? Why would the Arkham Knight use a drill machine to fight Batman? [/spoiler]These are just a couple of examples of the stupid scenarios the game puts you in. This brings me to the next problem the game has, memorable boss battles, because the game doesn’t have any. This is a huge disappointment since we got the terrifying Killer Croc battle in Asylum and creative Mr. Freeze battle in City. Boss battles either involve you doing beat em ups with another character or employs the use of the bat mobile, it isn’t fun and definitely not memorable, heck, there isn’t even a final boss battle which imo is really disappointing. The next problem the game has is the lack of a character arc, the only one worth mentioning is Batman’s, which is okay, but this means the rest of the characters get set aside. What made the villains in Asylum and City so memorable is that they have character arcs and interesting side quests that gets you to learn more about them, side missions in this game are the same missions over and over that leads to a boss battle that leads to Batman putting them in jail, end of story. 

In conclusion, the game is fun and plays well if you’re just looking to play as Batman, but if you have been a fan of the Arkham series like I’ve been; the game falls short, but is an okay sendoff to the beloved Arkham series.

Let’s talk about the flaws first.

[b] Batmobile: [/b] It doesn’t handle smooth. The game also relies heavily on the vehicle. It’s not a racing game so I would have really loved if they toned down the batmobile dependency.

[b] Story: [/b] Superb plot with really fleshed out characters. The voice acting is impeccable.
[b] Gameplay: [/b] Several quality-of-life improvements from previous games. Core gameplay is smooth and keeps you playing for hours. Grappling up to glide over Gotham City is an extraordinary feeling and makes traversal fun. It’s also fast so you don’t even miss the lack of fast travelling.

[h2]'A near perfect Batman experience slightly marred by a lack of originality in plot and overuse of the infamous bat-tank"[/h2]


   If you want to be the Batman, this is the ideal game. You can fight criminals and break their bones in ten different ways or prey on their fears and pick them one by one just like in previous Arkham games but this time your arsenal is superior, the stakes are higher and the playground is larger than ever. 

[b]Exploration[/b]

You finally have all of the Gotham for yourself, after being restricted to asylums and parts of the city in the prequels. The open world is spread over 3 distinctive islands, several times the size of Arkham City's map. You can glide through the night sky or use the newly introduced Batmobile to traverse the crime infested streets. I didn't find the controversial Batmobile clunky, it handles perfectly well. Of course the game sets it as the mandatory mode to travel in most parts, but if you are a fan of vehicular games, you will like it.

[b]Combat[/b] 

  Our favourite masked vigilante dons a new suit fitted with more sophisticated gadgets and he looks more intimidating than ever. Accordingly to match him, more advanced enemy types are introduced now and you can't just freeflow through an entire room easily like in City because these guys hit hard and fast. You are encouraged to be wary, use all the combat moves in your arsenal and dodge a lot. Also you can now interact with environmental objects for some slick encounters and in scripted events join up with your batbuddies and engage in cooperative attacks, all of which are cool.

[b]Stealth[/b]

 Predator encounters are filled with more new tactics, which brings a fresh breath of air into the game. Introducing fear takedowns and voice manipulation certainly enhances 'The Batman Mode' but it kind of make the whole thing easier, a little bit less challenging than City. Still I prefer the good old 'batclaw an enemy over a ledge or send one flying off a train roof with a batarang' tricks you could do in City. Sadly there are not many opportunities to do those here.


[b]Vehicular combat[/b]

   Its not bad as people say, in fact I enjoyed it. Just remember to put Battle mode setting to toggle mode in control options when you get the chance, it will make the whole thing fun and easy. Batmobile handles smoothly and combat is entertaining. So why did I say it was overused in the caption of the review? Because it overstays its welcome in the latter part of the game and is used shamelessly to fight [i]a certain antihero[/i] in a recycled boss battle which totally ruins the chance to see him and Batman going toe to toe in hand to hand combat for the second time in the series, but this time when both of them have evolved more. That would have been a  battle for ages to remember. I'm still sore about that missed chance.


[b]Story[/b]

   Its great, just not the best. Certainly a notch below Asylum, City and Origins. Luckily gameplay compensates for lack of creativity in the story. I'm not going into it much, I will just say a whole new character should have been the titular Arkham knight.
   Apart from that, story is a smasher especially in relation to Batman's character. It highlights the inner struggles of Bruce Wayne's mind, his darker persona, the obsession with Joker and the sacrifices he had to make over the years. And it gives a fitting end to Arkham Batman's legacy. ([i]It shouldn't have been touched again but Rocksteady did it anyway and we all know how it went[/i])
  Voice acting is at its prime as ever. Batman and Joker delivers as usual, but who captivated me most this time is The Riddler. He had me in stitches more than once with his lines.
 


[b]Content[/b]

But what Arkham Knight does best is giving lots of content to 'Be The Batman". Rocksteady certainly delivers on that premise. Side quests bring old and new villains into the limelight and they were great to complete and didn't feel tacked on. And they doesn't break the flow of main story. Riddler trophies and challenges may feel either interestingly challenging or incredibly annoying depending on your take on them. In addition to the story, there are lots of combat maps, predator maps and batmobile encounters. Even after doing all the achievements, you still have lots of AR challenges left you can do in your free time. DLC were a great addition, especially Season Of Infamy, which I think should have been incorporated to the main story because they were so good and brings closure to several important rogue gallery members' story arcs. Story packs which feature members of batfamily often get mixed reactions. Nevertheless I enjoyed the chance to play as those characters, short as some of them were. 

  If you are a hardcore Batman and a movie fan, the game gives you lots of additional treats in the form of cosmetic skins, both for batman and batmobile. You can now roleplay as your favourite Batman actor, be it Keaton, Bale, Affleck or Pattingson ([i]I'm a batbale fan myself[/i]) and drive around Gotham in their iconic batmobiles. I love this detail, its cherry on top for The ultimate Batman Experience.


[b]Graphics[/b]

  Not an essential for me and not an expert either, but for a 2015 game, this game looks terrific.

 In summary, [b]Arkham Knight is a fitting end to one of greatest and critically acclaimed game series with a few flaws that you can safely ignore and it is the definitive Batman experience currently existing in the game world.[/b]

I have mixed feelings about the game. On one hand, I can absolutely feel the love Rocksteady put into the game and it is a solid game in a general sense. On the other hand, some strange design choices undermine their efforts and leave a bad taste in the mouth. It is not as good as previous Arkham games.

I will touch on an actual flawed design first. The gameplay of Arkham Knight is the same as previous games, but adds car fight into the formula – you now can drive the iconic Batmobile to “even the odds”. The control of Batmobile will take a bit of time to get used to because it has two modes with drastically different control schemes, which is not a big problem. The problem is in pursue mode – it doesn’t turn as soon as you desire to. It is fine most of the time, as you can transform into tank mode in no time to maneuver it. But the game has a few obstacle-crossing sessions where the unresponsiveness becomes quite obvious and annoying, like the showdown with Arkham Knight.

The unresponsiveness is just a tiny problem compared to a few design choices regarding side quests, which I consider as the worst part of the game. For side quests, you are to catch villains and take over outposts. It sounds fine until you realize most (not all) quests are just repeating one specific gameplay consecutively. For instance, in Penguin's quest, you need to tail and brawl with thugs five times to finish. The same goes for outpost taking and most other villains. It doesn’t play bad, but repeating the same thing in a row is very tedious. I wish they would have mixed up the gameplay. Additionally, there are generally not enough stories attached to these quests to be engaging, making them more of mechanical repetition.

Some side quests have quite questionable designs if being mechanical is not bad enough. For the outpost and some villain hunt missions, you need to actively patrol Gotham to search their locations, otherwise, they won’t show up. It makes sense in logical terms but doesn’t change the fact that it is a very boring and time-wasting design. Also, these villains can only be traced by sound. The game doesn’t visualize sound into soundwave on the display, but asking you to literally hear it, which is such a bizarre design. Gotham is a giant map and it is already hard to find things by eye, now you also need to do that by ear. It doesn’t strike me as a smart design.

Even worse, you must finish all side quests to reveal the true ending of the game, meaning they are not really “optional”, among which you must collect 243 WELL-HIDDEN Riddler trophies. Anyone who has played this game will tell you it is a gigantic pain in the butt and too grindy to be fun. I ended up cheating by importing a save file to skip the trophy hunt. If you want to do all side quests yourself, it is going to be a massive time waste and downright impossible without walkthroughs.

It occurs to me that many games of Warner Interactive have similar grindy designs as if they are required to prolong playtime to a certain extent. I can get behind the rationale but it is usually not good for the experience. I appreciate most trophies contain a small, interesting puzzle and most side quests have decent levels, and I honestly think they overachieved by packing so many into the game. But unfortunately, it doesn’t elevate but harms the experience since I don’t feel my time is well-spent with these mechanical and repetitive side quests.

Since Arkham Origins, the series started putting focus on the character depth of Batman. I enjoyed it in Arkham Origins and think it really elevates the story. They do the same in Arkham Knight, but it is not as good. I have a hard time thinking about why, but I think ultimately it comes down to the supporting characters. In this game, Batman mainly shows his character depth by interacting with his allies and rivals under the influence of fear gas, but the supporting characters are not well developed, feeling like cardboard. It is like clapping doesn’t sound loud without echoes, and people say a great villain makes a great hero. For example, the Arkham Knight is supposed to be the second/third important character in the story, but his background and motive are introduced ever so slightly that it can’t reflect any greatness of the opposite force, Batman. The absence of well-established side characters makes the character of Batman feels somewhat hollow and not as satisfying as before. But that is just my nitpicking and my theory.

There are some other downsides I can point out: the Batwoman DLC crashed three times for no reason whereas the rest of the game run completely fine; there is some poor and gimmicky level design in Gotham Episodes DLC; the realistic art style doesn’t look as good as the previous more cartoon-ish style on female characters; optimization is mediocre. But these are not as significant to the experience as those mentioned above. Again, even with those flaws, it is still a solid game. I enjoyed being Batman, the action, the story, the gorgeous view of Gotham and particularly, the presentation is so superb that it gives me goosebumps. I really wish they would have picked better design choices for side quests.

I'm not a hardcore Batman fan, but I absolutely love Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight (2008) and Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker (I even made a Joker parody back in 2014 where Batman calls me on Skype, although the video is private now). I'm also a veteran of Batman: Arkham Asylum (2009), which I first played back in my school days with my classmates (who were huge Batman and Hitman fans).

Arkham Asylum (2009) set a completely new standard for the gaming industry, especially with its seamless Freeflow combat system. After its success, many other franchises—such as Assassin's Creed, Marvel's Spider-Man, and others—adopted similar fluid combat mechanics and design ideas. Back then, NVIDIA PhysX was one of the coolest technologies in PC gaming. I still remember how not every graphics card could handle it properly in games like this. Even back then, I absolutely loved the technology, and I was pleasantly surprised to see it implemented in Batman: Arkham Asylum (2009). The paper debris, cloth physics, smoke, particles, and destructible environmental effects looked incredible at the time and made the world feel much more alive. It was one of those features that truly felt "next-gen." Arkham Asylum is a truly legendary game. It received outstanding reviews from both critics and players, and in my opinion, it fully deserved every bit of its Game of the Year recognition.

[h1]What about Batman: Arkham Knight (2015)?[/h1]
[b]Well... this is the final Batman game from Rocksteady, and it brings together everything the previous games did well. It features the Batmobile, significantly improves the cinematic presentation with outstanding animations, lighting, reflections, and visual effects, and honestly, it still looks incredibly modern even in 2026. Arkham Knight runs on a heavily modified version of Unreal Engine 3. Rocksteady Studios pushed the technology of this engine far beyond its original capabilities, extensively reworking and improving it to create the open-world Gotham City. Thanks to these advancements, the game still looks visually impressive and remains on par with many modern-generation titles even today.My first reaction was:[/b] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uvsPzuriDdA [b]...and that's coming from someone who's been familiar with the Arkham series for years. If someone asked me to recommend just one Batman game, this would be my answer without hesitation Arkham Knight (2015) because it still looks absolutely incredible today. That said, Arkham Asylum (2009) still has a unique charm of its own. Today, I'd recommend playing both if you want to experience where this legendary series began.[/b]

[h2]My ranking of all Arkham games[/h2]
If you've never played a Batman game before, here's how I'd rank them for you:

[h3]🥇 1. Batman: Arkham Knight (2015)[/h3]
It still looks like a game that could have been released yesterday. The visuals are just as stunning and juicy as those in Need for Speed (2015). The gameplay offers the most variety, there are tons of mechanics, side activities, and overall it's the most complete Arkham experience. [b]It has the fastest and most satisfying gliding mechanics in the entire series. Pure joy.[/b]

[h3]🥈 2. Batman: Arkham Asylum (2009)[/h3]
A true Game of the Year classic that changed the gaming industry. Its Freeflow combat system inspired countless games that followed. I'd compare its influence to what The Matrix did for action movies—it introduced ideas that many others would later build upon.

[h3]🥉 3. Batman: Arkham City (2011)[/h3]
Another deserved Game of the Year winner. It expands everything from Asylum with a much larger open-world environment, plenty of side content, and... over 400 Riddler trophies (good luck with those 😅). I only wish there had been more Catwoman gameplay, since her playable sections are surprisingly limited (only 4 playable story chapters).

[h3]🤷🏻‍♂️ 4. Batman: Arkham Origins (2013)[/h3]
This prequel was developed by a different studio, and you can feel that almost immediately. Batman comes across as surprisingly sadistic, both in the way he talks to people and in the way he treats them. That was my first impression. Personally, I'd rank it last. I wasn't a fan of how Batman and Joker were portrayed, both visually and in terms of their personalities. If graphics are your main concern, don't assume this game looks better than the previous entries, simply because it came out later than Arkham City. In my opinion, City and even Asylum still hold up just as well—and in some scenes, they actually look better. I'd recommend treating Arkham Origins as its own standalone project instead of directly comparing it to the Rocksteady trilogy. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3770838160

First of all - I am not a big fan of Batman or superhero universes at all. Besides Nolan trilogy, or the first 2 Tim Burton movies, I haven't seen any of the other movies,  watched TV series, read comic books or even played that many video games with Batman.

So I don't want to say that I was sceptical about it, maybe I just went in with some lower expectations. But all that being said, I really do appreciate a good game, cause if the game is  good - then all of the above really does not matter. 

I played only Arkham Asylum (out of all Batman games in the existence), which I really enjoyed. I didn't expect that an open world game where you are running around on a million of quests is going to be on the same level of quality. But Arkham Knight really is. Maybe even better in some ways.

Arkham Knight was ignored from my side because of the things mentioned above, but also because of its poor PC launch. Today, the game is running as it should and is looking fantastic while doing it (it really is one of the best looking games ever made). It has so much quality in the terms of lightning, atmosphere building, good colour palette and slight film grain, with a lot of attention to detail.

Voice acting was done also on the highest level, and the music is giving me that 90's Batman vibe, which for me, sets the tone perfectly. 

Gameplay itself is pretty solid, although it has some of the things that could've been executed better - there are to be honest, too many tank fights (although they are good), there are logical puzzles that can get a bit annoying, and of course some of the stuff can be a bit repetitive (like clearing the city from the mines, or bunkers) - its an open world game and I kinda expected that. But overall, once you get the hang of it, you will become one with the Dark Knight and you will move around the Gotham fluently and you will probably enjoy it, because for the most of the time - it is really fun.

I didn't like the logic and the execution of the Riddler segment, because it felt unrealistic, arcady and it felt like those challenges didn't fit the tone of the game (all the ones with the car at least). But everything else in the story was really on point. It was dark and serious, with some twists and turns that I just didnt expect. Of course, again, you have to finish 250 of Riddler challenges to see the true ending - which for me is a no-go, so I just Youtubed the last 5 minutes of the "true" ending. That also can be a negative point, hiding the ending after getting all the collectibles. 

But, all in all, Arkham Knight was a really good, enjoyable, fun experience and I am glad that I gave it a chance. The price during the sale was really low, and you can get a lot of quality content out of this game.

Very much recommended for all the Batman fans out there, but also for people who are not fans, but can respect a really good game. Or if you are just into open world games, this is one of the best open worlds there is.

This game is simply amazing. My favourite of the 4 Batman games.

+ Visuals: the amount of detail in the world and the characters is mind-boggling. This game looks like a tech demo; it's impressive as fuck to look at and runs great.

+ Gameplay: It's incredibly polished, varied, engaging, and FUN. Whether you like action brawlers or open world games you will love this one. The combat is as fluid and tight as ever; you feel like the ultimate badass. The combat system is the perfect mix of accessible and deep. I've heard complaints about the vehicle sections being tedious or annoying or just poorly designed but I quite enjoyed them. The addition of the batmobile and how they designed its functionality is very well done.

+ Sound: Top-notch. The sound of the batmobile is just wicked awesome, and the voice acting is just superb. After being disappointed with the voice actor they used as Batman for Arkham Origins I'm glad they got Kevin Conroy back. He's incredible. The original score is so good it rivals Hans Zimmers score(s) from the Dark Knight Trilogy.

+ Content: Open-world collectathons kinda turn me off and I don't like being a janitor cleaning up a virtual world littered with pointless objects to collect, so that's why I've completed literally everything except the Riddler trophies. Thankfully most of the other missions are structured in a way that's fun and varied so you feel like you're accomplishing something rather than just mindlessly collecting things (yes I understand that some riddler trophies require you to think with puzzle solving). The amount of DLC available now is also fantastic, lots of varied skins offer a welcome visual variety to the game, which I thoroughly enjoyed; Ben Afflecks Batman suit fits this game/world perfectly imo.

Overall: This is one of the best games I've ever played. The direction, cinematics, gameplay, score, voice acting, characters, setting...it's all incredible and made with care and a love for the source material. Sure, you can get all the Batman Arkham games and play them through for additional context, but if you're looking for THE definitive Batman gaming experience then just get this game and 100% it; you will not regret it!
